extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in public opinion, media, and political communication
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and conceptual criteria for analyzing how public opinion is formed and how news/images in people's minds influence political behavior. Emphasizes the relation between representations (pictures) and real-world action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictures in our heads / pseudo-environment
rubrics_metrics.description: People act not upon the real environment but upon a 'picture' or 'pseudo-environment' — the mental image of events and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To analyze public opinion, examine the contents of these pictures: what image of the scene people hold, how it was formed, and how behavior is a response to that pseudo-environment. Examples: islanders acting on stale newspaper accounts; senators responding to a possibly false dispatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangular relationship: scene, picture, response
rubrics_metrics.description: Public behavior arises from a triangular relation among the real scene of action, the human picture of that scene, and the human response which is worked out upon the scene of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation must consider all three corners — the objective facts, the representations people hold, and the resulting actions — because consequences play out in the real environment even when motives are formed in the pseudo-environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of fidelity of fictions / usefulness of models
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictions and schematic models have varying degrees of fidelity, ranging from hallucination to the scientist's schematic model; they are not necessarily lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess representations by their degree of fidelity and functional adequacy for the task at hand (e.g., when precision beyond certain decimals is unnecessary). Recognize that useful simplifications can guide action if their limits are understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and the interval between perception and reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The speed at which news reaches people — sometimes fast, sometimes slow — creates intervals during which people act on outdated or inaccurate pictures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how timing and delay affect adjustments to events (maladjustment), e.g., plans made under an obsolete picture of the world; consider the role of 'time and attention' in shaping public reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source credibility and deliberate manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Information sources (including intentionally deceptive dispatches) shape the pictures people adopt; deliberate fraud or partisan reporting can manufacture pseudo-environments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check provenance and motive of information; investigate rather than assume rumors as facts. Example: a dispatch intended to defeat the League of Nations produced a false picture that influenced Senate debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols, stereotypes, and the organization of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic pictures (heroes, devils, stereotypes) condense complex realities into emotionally charged images that organize feelings and conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether symbolic images are inclusive or fragmentary, how strongly they suppress individual differences, and whether they are subject to checks and argument (stronger in peacetime, totalizing in wartime).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps-of-the-world metaphor: simplification vs. distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: People need 'maps of the world' — simplified reconstructions — to act; these maps are often sketched to satisfy someone's need and can misrepresent reality (e.g., maps with 'coast of Bohemia').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze who sketched the map (whose needs), what has been omitted or exaggerated, and the practical consequences of acting on that map.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interests and the formation of belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs and images are often shaped by interests (self-interest, class interest, national interest) and by organized efforts (propaganda) to form group consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating public opinion, identify which interests are being enlisted or transferred, and how propaganda substitutes one social pattern for another (e.g., class consciousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment and maladjustment (consequences of divergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the pseudo-environment diverges from the real environment, action based on the false picture leads to maladjustment and cognitive dissonance — 'butting one's head against a stone wall.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the gap between representation and reality and trace resulting failures or unintended consequences; use examples of war-time misperceptions and post-armistice continuing losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public persona construction vs. private reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Great men and public figures commonly exist as constructed public personalities distinct from private selves; media and popular expectation often create façades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate journalistic and biographical representations for stage-managed elements versus genuine interior life; beware of portraits that are 'epic' abstractions rather than realistic biographies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality, competition, and the balancing of interests
rubrics_metrics.description: In normal public life, multiple competing symbols and interests produce conflict, choice, and compromise rather than a single unified public will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a particular symbolic picture dominates (e.g., wartime unity) or whether the field of opinion shows check, comparison, and argument; this affects how durable and representative public opinion is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function versus truth: social role of inaccurate beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some fictions, though inaccurate, serve social or psychological functions (comfort, mobilization, explanation) and therefore persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging representations, consider both their truth-value and their functional role in social cohesion, motivation, or control; differentiate harmful mal-adjusting fictions from useful simplifying conventions.
